title: Statement and Argument and Inference: Judging Reasons and Conclusions

questions.question: Statement: Should exams be conducted online? Argument: No — my cousin failed an online exam last year, so online exams are unfair. This argument is:
options: Strong — it cites a real case
Weak — online exams are actually fair
questions.rationale: A single relative's failure cannot support a claim about all exams — the argument fails the representativeness filter. Note the fourth option commits the sin of importing your own opinion instead of judging reasoning quality.

questions.question: Which of these is a CIRCULAR argument in a debate on banning private tuition?
options: Tuition should be banned because tutoring outside school is wrong
Tuition should be banned because it costs parents dearly
Tuition should not be banned because coaching employs lakhs
Tuition should not be banned because classroom sizes are large
questions.rationale: The circular option assumes the very conclusion (that such tutoring is wrong) as its premise. The others offer external, testable grounds — cost, employment, classroom conditions — which may be strong or weak but at least engage the issue.

questions.question: Statement: All applicants who cleared the interview had either a postgraduate degree or three years of experience. Ravi cleared the interview. What DEFINITELY follows?
options: Ravi has three years of experience
Ravi has both a degree and experience
questions.rationale: Clearing the interview forces having been interviewed — but the either/or clause leaves the degree-versus-experience branch undetermined. Options 1, 2, and 4 all smuggle in a branch the statement never pins down.

questions.question: Statement: All diabetics are patients; some patients are children. Which conclusion follows?
questions.rationale: All A are B validly converts to some B are A — so some patients are diabetics. The 'some-some' chain proves nothing about diabetic children, and reversing a 'some' (option 2) is the classic illicit conversion.

questions.question: 'All A are B; x is not B' — what validly follows?
questions.rationale: This is modus tollens: if every A is inside B, and x lies outside B, then x cannot be an A. The invalid sibling, denying the antecedent ('x is not A, so x is not B'), is the exam's favourite wrong option.

questions.question: Statement: The municipal corporation will fine any household with an illegal water connection, after a survey beginning next month. Which inference is DEFININITELY true?
options: Households surveyed after the survey begins can be fined
All illegal connections will be found
questions.rationale: The fine's trigger is mechanical: any household with an illegal connection, once the survey is underway — so post-survey fining is definitely true. Whether violations exist (option 1) is only probable, and motive (option 2) is speculation.

questions.question: An argument saying 'this policy should be rejected because it will ALWAYS fail everywhere it is tried' is weakened primarily by:
questions.rationale: 'Always' and 'everywhere' make the claim refutable by a single counterexample — the proportion and tone filters mark such absolutism as weak unless overwhelming evidence is supplied.

questions.question: In statement-and-inference questions, bringing in your own outside knowledge is:
options: Forbidden — the statement is a closed universe
questions.rationale: Every inference must be graded purely on what the statement says. If the statement is silent, the answer is 'data inadequate' — no matter how true your outside fact feels, it cannot upgrade a conclusion.

questions.question: Statement: Some cats are black; some black things are dogs. What follows about cats and dogs?
questions.rationale: Two 'some' statements share only the middle term (black things) — the overlap regions may or may not intersect. Neither a positive nor a negative link between cats and dogs is forced.

questions.question: A strong argument in the online-exams debate would be:
options: Online exams are bad because screens are modern
Online exams halve evaluation time per paper, as pilot results from 50 colleges show
questions.rationale: It is relevant, representative (50 colleges, not one cousin), evidenced (pilot data), proportionate, and measured — passing all five filters. Vague modernity complaints, appeals to common knowledge, and single-person anecdotes fail them.
